matches.section: 2.2 Coordinate Frames and Scene Calibration
matches.text: The reconstruction of Chapter 6 is drawn in the Unity frame, the display axes of that chapter. It shares the desk marker origin of the world frame and exchanges the second and third coordinates, so its y axis points up and it is left-handed. Chapter 6 converts every pose into it before it draws anything. Those display axes are not levelled and stay anchored on the desk marker. The coordinate system of the finished scene in Figure 2.4(b) is the same axes turned upright by the calibrated gravity direction and dropped so that the drawn floor is at zero height. Section 6.4 builds both steps.

matches.section: 5.1 Assumptions and Parameters
matches.text: The recovery needs parameters of three kinds, each stated where its rule is defined. The calibrated constants are the upper-arm and forearm lengths, taken from the clean frames at the start of the recording or from an earlier calibration. They also include the fixed mapping derived from the scene calibration, swap and levelling, which carries a point of {Levelled} into {Camera'} (Section 5.3). The design values were fixed before the recording. They are the detector thresholds and the mask cleaning of Section 5.2, the gains, radii, entry and exit runs and memory horizon of Section 5.3, the offset bound of Section 5.4, and the reach guard, twist hold and rate limit of Section 5.5. The states are estimated on clean frames of the recording and carried forward: the hand-object offset per grip episode, the holding state of each hand, and the direction memories of the two arms. No parameter is fitted on a flagged frame.

matches.section: 5.4 Wrist Recovery from the Object Pose
matches.text: The estimate ​Levelledw is a function of a same-frame measurement, and only the offset is carried from the past, on the short memory of Section 5.3. A wrist placed from its last direction stays near where the arm was when tracking failed and drifts the longer the window lasts, while the object-derived wrist follows the cube through the whole window and does not age. Case B therefore takes priority over Case A whenever the hand holds the cube and the marker is measured.

matches.section: 5.4 Wrist Recovery from the Object Pose
matches.text: The frames need one conversion step. The wrist estimate of equation (5.7) is formed in the levelled frame {Levelled}, which Section 6.4 establishes, while the solve works in the y-up camera frame {Camera'} of Chapter 3. The fixed rigid body transformation LevelledCamera'T of the scene calibration (Section 2.2.2) therefore carries the estimate into the y-up camera frame before the solve. It changes no length and no angle.

matches.section: 6.4 Scene Reconstruction in Unity
matches.text: That rotation defines the levelled frame. The levelled frame keeps the origin and the handedness of the Unity frame of equation (6.1), whose axes this chapter calls the display axes, and its upward axis is the calibrated gravity direction. Written with both of its frames the rotation is UnityLevelledR, which is proper, so the levelling turns the reconstruction without changing the handedness of the frame.

matches.text: The receiver then raises the whole reconstruction so that the drawn floor sits at zero height. That raise defines the scene frame, the coordinate system Unity itself draws in. The scene frame carries the axes of the levelled frame exactly, because the raise turns nothing, and its origin sits on the drawn floor, a vertical distance d below the origin of the levelled frame. matches.section: 7.2 Object Reconstruction Accuracy
matches.text: The measured point is the ArUco marker centre on the cube face, at both physically measured endpoints and in the reconstruction. The physical separations are tape measurements made by the author between marker-centre positions, at a resolution of 1 millimetre, and the physical setup is the same in both recordings. The physical route is not registered into the world frame of the desk-marker calibration, nor into the levelled frame derived from it, so no physical path or physical waypoint coordinate is drawn or reported.

matches.text: Segment lengths are invariant under the levelling rotation that carries the display axes of equation (6.1) into the levelled frame, because that rotation is proper and preserves distance, so the choice between the two frames cannot change Tables 7.1 and 7.2. The fitted-line scatter components, the line tilt and the axis-dominance checks used to confirm that each waypoint sits in its intended task phase are properties of the levelled frame and are not invariant.

matches.section: 7.3 Human Reconstruction Accuracy under Valid Landmark Measurements
matches.text: The corresponding Unity joints are the forearm bone head for the elbow and the hand bone head for the wrist. Their saved world positions include display filtering and rig mapping. The calibrated camera mapping, gravity levelling and recording-specific floor translation carry the measured landmarks into {Scene}, where the logged rig joints are expressed. The {Levelled} coordinates used elsewhere share these axes but omit the floor translation. Frame identifiers match exactly, and timestamp and pelvis correspondence checks verify the saved capture. For joint k at frame t, positional error is

matches.section: 7.3 Human Reconstruction Accuracy under Valid Landmark Measurements
matches.text: Reconstruction places the wrist a median of 15.77 centimetres from the marker centre while the right hand holds the cube alone, and 14.08 centimetres while the left hand holds it alone. Both reconstructed positions are expressed in the levelled frame, and their separation is a distance, so it does not depend on that choice. Both medians sit within about two centimetres of the physical reference, so the reconstructed human-object separation is of the correct magnitude.
